title: Shopify Plus Cross-Border Repeat Customer Growth: The 149% Benchmark
summary: Shopify Plus cross-border repeat customer growth benchmarks: the 149% Her lip to result, APAC retention data, and a 90-day plan for beauty and fashion brands.
body_markdown:
**Quick Answer:** Shopify Plus cross-border repeat customer growth is driven by configuration, not advertising. Shopify's case study on Her lip to reports a 149% repeat-customer increase and roughly 400% cross-border revenue growth after migration — achieved through duties at checkout, market pricing, local payments and localised lifecycle flows.


---


Most brands treat cross-border as an acquisition problem. It isn't. The most-cited number in Shopify Plus cross-border repeat customer growth — the 149% increase in repeat customers reported in Shopify's published case study on Haruna Kojima's fashion label Her lip to — did not come from buying traffic in new markets. It came from making the second purchase easy for people who had already bought once. Same catalogue, same brand equity, different plumbing.


*Related reading:*[Shopify Plus AI Commerce Standards: UCP Across APAC Markets](https://branch8.com/posts/shopify-plus-ai-commerce-standards-ucp-apac)


*Related reading:*[Shopify ChapGPT Integration for E-Commerce Selling in APAC](https://branch8.com/posts/shopify-chatgpt-integration-ecommerce-selling-apac)


I run a retail-services business out of Hong Kong that supports global beauty and luxury brands, and I see the same pattern in the pipeline reviews every quarter. Teams budget six figures for market-entry paid media, then send a Japanese or Australian first-time buyer a post-purchase email in English, priced in USD, with no visible duty estimate and a support inbox that answers 14 hours later. That's not a demand problem. That's an operations problem, and operations problems are the cheap ones to fix.


*Related reading:*[Salesforce AWS Partnership Global Growth: The APAC Playbook](https://branch8.com/posts/salesforce-aws-partnership-global-growth-apac)


*Related reading:*[L'Oréal CDP Implementation Retail ROI: What the Data Shows](https://branch8.com/posts/loreal-cdp-implementation-retail-roi-benchmarks)


*Related reading:*[Google Invests in Anthropic: AI Implications for APAC Teams](https://branch8.com/posts/google-invests-anthropic-ai-implications-apac)


Here's what the data says, and what the benchmarks should be for APAC beauty and fashion brands going into 2026.


## The 149% figure is a retention outcome, not a traffic outcome


Shopify's case study on Her lip to reports two headline results after the brand migrated to Shopify Plus: a 149% increase in repeat customers and roughly a 400% increase in cross-border revenue. Read those two numbers together. Cross-border revenue quadrupling while repeat customers grow at 149% tells you the growth was compounding on an existing base, not resetting with each campaign.


That matters because the maths of cross-border are brutal on first orders. Higher shipping cost, duty exposure, FX spread, elevated return rates, and lower conversion on unfamiliar payment methods all land on order number one. Order two is where the unit economics turn. A brand that can't reliably get to order two in an export market is renting revenue, not building it.


Shopify itself frames the opportunity in volume terms — its cross-border commerce guidance cites projections of global cross-border ecommerce exceeding US$4.81 trillion by 2032. The projection is directional. The operational question is which share of that you keep after CAC.


## Cross-border repeat rates lag domestic by a wide margin


Use these reference points when you build your own cross-border repeat customer growth plan:


### Benchmarks worth holding yourself to


- **Cart abandonment sets the ceiling.** Baymard Institute's aggregate of 51 studies puts average documented cart abandonment at 70.19%. In cross-border checkouts with no local payment method and no landed-cost display, real-world figures run worse — every abandoned cart is also a lost retention cohort.
- **Cross-border is a meaningful slice of Shopify GMV.** Shopify's Black Friday–Cyber Monday reporting has consistently shown cross-border orders at roughly 15% of total orders across the platform, on GMV that reached US$11.5 billion over the BFCM weekend in 2024 (Shopify Newsroom).
- **Payment coverage is now table stakes.** Shopify Payments is available in 39+ countries per Shopify's own documentation, with local payment methods surfaced by market. If you are still routing Japanese customers through a card-only checkout, you're leaving conversion on the table before retention even starts.
- **APAC is the volume centre.** Statista's ecommerce market data consistently places Asia-Pacific as the largest regional contributor to global retail ecommerce sales — which is why a US or UK brand's "international" plan and its "Asia" plan should not be the same document.
- **Beauty and fashion behave differently.** McKinsey's retail and State of Fashion research has repeatedly flagged replenishment-driven categories (skincare, cosmetics) as structurally higher-frequency than apparel. A 149% repeat lift in a fashion label is therefore a harder result than the same number in skincare.
- **Email and SMS carry the second order.** Klaviyo's published benchmark reporting shows lifecycle flows — welcome, post-purchase, replenishment, win-back — generating a disproportionate share of owned-channel revenue relative to campaign blasts. Cross-border brands that localise flows but not campaigns still capture most of the value.


If you want one crude target: your 90-day repeat purchase rate in an export market should reach at least 60% of your domestic rate within four quarters of launch. Below that, localisation is incomplete somewhere in the funnel.

## Four levers move the cross-border repeat rate


Every cross-border repeat customer growth strategy I've seen work in APAC pulls the same four levers, in roughly this order of ROI.


### 1. Landed cost clarity before checkout


Duties collected at the door are the single most reliable way to destroy a repeat customer. Shopify's Markets functionality supports duties and import tax collection at checkout, so the customer sees one number and the courier never surprises them. This is a configuration decision, not a development project — and it changes second-order intent more than any discount you can offer.


### 2. Market-level pricing, not FX conversion


Automatic currency conversion produces prices like ¥4,387. Shopify Markets supports price rounding rules and market-specific price lists. In Japan, Taiwan and Hong Kong, round-number psychological pricing is not cosmetic — it is the difference between a premium and a clearance read.


### 3. Delivery promise per market, honoured


A Hong Kong multi-brand beauty group we supported ran three separate 3PL relationships across HK, Taiwan and Singapore with different cut-off times, all displaying a single generic shipping message. The fix wasn't a new warehouse. It was market-specific delivery windows on the PDP and in the post-purchase email, matched to actual carrier cut-offs. Mechanically, you are removing the gap between promise and experience — that gap is what suppresses reorders.


### 4. Support hours that overlap the customer's day


This is where most US and EU brands quietly lose Asia. If your only support coverage is 9–6 in London or New York, a Tokyo or Sydney customer is waiting a full business day for a sizing answer. Distributed teams in Hong Kong, Taipei, Manila or Kuala Lumpur close that window at a fraction of onshore cost — and response latency is a retention input, not a cost line.


## Shopify Plus earns its price through market count, not features


The most common objection I hear from founders is the one the search results echo: why is Shopify Plus so expensive? Shopify's published pricing puts Plus in the low thousands of US dollars per month depending on term and volume — real money for a brand doing under US$2M.


The honest trade-off: if you sell in one market, one currency, one language, Plus is hard to justify on features alone. The economics change when market count rises. Multiple storefronts under Shopify Markets, expansion stores, higher API limits, Shopify Functions for market-specific checkout logic, and B2B on Shopify for wholesale in export markets are the things you cannot replicate cheaply on the standard plan. Plus is priced for portfolio complexity, and cross-border is portfolio complexity.


On the competitor question: Shopify's biggest platform rivals at enterprise level remain Adobe Commerce (Magento), Salesforce Commerce Cloud and BigCommerce, with SHOPLINE a serious contender specifically in Greater China and Southeast Asia because of its native social-commerce and local payment coverage. For APAC-first brands, the real evaluation is usually Shopify Plus versus SHOPLINE, not Shopify Plus versus Adobe.

## A 90-day cross-border repeat customer growth program


Pick one export market. Not three.


**Days 1–30 — instrument.** Split every retention metric by market: repeat purchase rate, time to second order, AOV, return rate, support first-response time. Most brands discover they have never seen these numbers by market, only in aggregate. Aggregate numbers hide the market that's bleeding.


**Days 31–60 — localise the transaction.** Duties at checkout, local payment methods enabled, market price lists with rounding, market-specific delivery windows, returns instructions in-language. All configuration, no rebuild.


**Days 61–90 — localise the lifecycle.** Translate and re-time your post-purchase, replenishment and win-back flows to local send windows. A replenishment email timed to New York mornings arrives at 9pm in Taipei.


Then measure time-to-second-order against your domestic baseline. That single metric tells you more about cross-border health than revenue does, because revenue can be bought and reorder speed can't.


## What to do Monday morning


1. **Pull your repeat purchase rate by market for the last 12 months.** If your analytics can't produce it in an hour, that's the first finding. Rank markets by repeat rate, not revenue.
2. **Place a test order as a customer in your largest export market.** Card in local currency, real address. Note every point where price, duty, delivery date or language breaks. That list is your Q1 roadmap.
3. **Check your support first-response time by customer timezone.** If APAC customers are waiting more than four working hours, price a distributed coverage model before you price another media buy.


Shopify Plus cross-border repeat customer growth is won in configuration and coverage, not in campaign budgets. The 149% benchmark exists because someone fixed the boring parts first.
